strengths: The method addresses an important practical problem: distilling large image datasets using feature representatives and per-class BatchNorm regularization without expensive bilevel optimization.

Table 1 reports substantial improvements at 50 images per class: 57.6% on ImageNet-1K versus 53.5% for the strongest listed baseline, and 59.4% on Tiny ImageNet versus 48.7%. Repeated runs with reported variability strengthen this empirical evidence.

Evaluation includes multiple compression budgets, transfer to ResNet and ViT architectures, factorial component ablations, and sensitivity studies. Table 4 supports consistent incremental benefits from feature matching when combined with PCBN.

The manuscript provides useful diagrams, algorithm descriptions, hyperparameter tables, and a code link, and attributes the datasets and underlying methods. The societal-impact discussion appropriately acknowledges that distillation can preserve source-data biases.
weaknesses: The novelty of the central optimization is insufficiently distinguished from standard clustering. With one input distribution, squared Euclidean transport cost, and freely optimized atom weights, Eqs. (5)–(8) reduce to the k-means objective: the average squared distance to the nearest representative. This connection should be acknowledged, and feature-space k-means with the same image inversion and PCBN should be compared. The multiple-distribution barycenter illustration does not establish an advantage for this particular formulation.

The headline improvements are difficult to attribute to the proposed components. On ImageNet-1K at 10 IPC, SRe2L scores 21.3% in Table 1, whereas the CE-plus-standard-BN configuration scores 35.9% in Table 4. Within Table 4, replacing CE with Wasserstein feature matching after adding PCBN improves 36.4% to 38.1%. The much larger baseline discrepancy needs explanation, including matched teacher, weighting, augmentation, and FKD settings.

The comparison against MMD does not adequately isolate the distribution metric. Removing augmentation and FKD does not establish equivalent encoders and regularization. With one representative per class and a fixed encoder, squared-Wasserstein minimization and linear-MMD matching both target the class feature mean, making the reported near-random MMD replacement particularly important to explain. Matched linear and characteristic-kernel comparisons are needed; Appendix B's generic risk bounds do not resolve this empirical confounding.

The barycenter algorithm has unresolved correctness and reproducibility details. Algorithm 2 updates the weights but reuses the transport plan computed for the previous weights, which does not justify the claimed position update under the new marginals. Simplex projection also permits zero weights, while Eq. (11) divides by those weights. Initialization, the weight-update learning rate, zero-weight handling, and the precise use of weights during FKD should be specified.

The comparative efficiency evidence is limited to ImageNette at 1 IPC, where the representative is simply the feature mean. Although ImageNet experiments demonstrate feasibility, they do not quantify the claimed efficiency advantage at realistic larger budgets. A comparable runtime and memory breakdown covering teacher training, feature extraction, transport, image recovery, and relabeling would substantiate the practical savings.
